claim: Aging individuals exhibit a pervasive decline in adaptive immune function, with important implications for health and lifespan.
source: Aging individuals exhibit a pervasive decline in adaptive immune function, with important implications for health and lifespan.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Previous studies have found a pervasive loss of immune-repertoire diversity in human peripheral blood during aging.
source: Previous studies have found a pervasive loss of immune-repertoire diversity in human peripheral blood during aging
evidence: This statement references prior research findings, as indicated by citations in the introduction.

claim: Little is known about repertoire aging in other immune compartments, or in species other than humans.
source: however, little is known about repertoire aging in other immune compartments, or in species other than humans.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on review of existing literature.

claim: This is the first study of immune-repertoire aging in the African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri).
source: Here, we perform the first study of immune-repertoire aging in an emerging model of vertebrate aging, the African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri).
evidence: The authors explicitly state this is the first such study in this species.

claim: Turquoise killifish have extremely short lifespans.
source: Despite their extremely short lifespans, these killifish exhibit complex and individualized heavy-chain repertoires
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Turquoise killifish exhibit complex and individualized heavy-chain repertoires.
source: Despite their extremely short lifespans, these killifish exhibit complex and individualized heavy-chain repertoires, with a generative process capable of producing millions of distinct productive sequences.
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data and analysis presented in the results.

claim: The killifish generative process is capable of producing millions of distinct productive sequences.
source: Despite their extremely short lifespans, these killifish exhibit complex and individualized heavy-chain repertoires, with a generative process capable of producing millions of distinct productive sequences.
evidence: This is calculated from the generative model analysis showing ~23 bits of productive entropy, corresponding to ~10^7 sequences.

claim: Whole-body killifish repertoires decline rapidly in within-individual diversity with age.
source: Whole-body killifish repertoires decline rapidly in within-individual diversity with age, while between-individual variability increases.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the alpha-diversity spectra analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Between-individual variability in killifish repertoires increases with age.
source: Whole-body killifish repertoires decline rapidly in within-individual diversity with age, while between-individual variability increases.
evidence: This is shown by beta-diversity spectra and RDI distance analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Large, expanded B-cell clones exhibit far greater diversity loss with age than small clones.
source: Large, expanded B-cell clones exhibit far greater diversity loss with age than small clones, suggesting important differences in how age affects different B-cell populations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing VJ diversity spectra for large vs. small clones in Figure 2D-F.

claim: The immune repertoires of isolated intestinal samples exhibit especially dramatic age-related diversity loss.
source: The immune repertoires of isolated intestinal samples exhibit especially dramatic age-related diversity loss, related to an elevated prevalence of expanded clones.
evidence: This is shown by the intestinal repertoire analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Intestinal age-related diversity loss is related to an elevated prevalence of expanded clones.
source: The immune repertoires of isolated intestinal samples exhibit especially dramatic age-related diversity loss, related to an elevated prevalence of expanded clones.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rarefaction analysis and clone-size distribution comparisons in Figure 5.

claim: Lower intestinal repertoire diversity was associated with transcriptomic signatures of reduced B-cell activity.
source: Lower intestinal repertoire diversity was also associated with transcriptomic signatures of reduced B-cell activity, supporting a functional role for diversity changes in killifish immunosenescence.
evidence: This is shown by gene set enrichment analysis in Figure 6.

claim: There are important differences in systemic vs. organ-specific aging dynamics in the adaptive immune system.
source: Our results highlight important differences in systemic vs. organ-specific aging dynamics in the adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing whole-body and intestinal repertoire aging patterns.

claim: Aging is accompanied by a decline in naïve B-cell output from the primary lymphoid organs.
source: In the humoral immune system, aging is accompanied by a decline in naïve B-cell output from the primary lymphoid organs; impaired production of specific antibodies in response to antigenic challenge; and a decline in antibody quality (Ademokun et al., 2010; Kogut et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2011; Aberle et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Aging is accompanied by impaired production of specific antibodies in response to antigenic challenge.
source: In the humoral immune system, aging is accompanied by a decline in naïve B-cell output from the primary lymphoid organs; impaired production of specific antibodies in response to antigenic challenge; and a decline in antibody quality (Ademokun et al., 2010; Kogut et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2011; Aberle et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Aging is accompanied by a decline in antibody quality.
source: In the humoral immune system, aging is accompanied by a decline in naïve B-cell output from the primary lymphoid organs; impaired production of specific antibodies in response to antigenic challenge; and a decline in antibody quality (Ademokun et al., 2010; Kogut et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2011; Aberle et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Aging is accompanied by impairments in the establishment of novel immune memory.
source: as well as impairments in the establishment of novel immune memory (Aberle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: These immunosenescent changes are major contributors to impaired health and quality of life in the elderly.
source: These changes are major contributors to a generalized immunosenescent phenotype that significantly impairs health and quality of life in the elderly.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The efficacy of the humoral immune system rests on its ability to generate an enormous array of different antibody sequences.
source: The efficacy of the humoral immune system rests on its ability to generate an enormous array of different antibody sequences, with a correspondingly vast range of antigen specificities, and to progressively adjust the composition of this antibody population in response to antigen exposure (Schatz and Swanson, 2011; Di Noia and Neuberger, 2007; Magor, 2015; Elhanati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences with age.
source: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a number of important age-related changes, including reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences, increased baseline mutation, more frequent and larger clonal expansions, impaired B-cell selection, and a shift toward the memory compartment (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered increased baseline mutation with age.
source: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a number of important age-related changes, including reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences, increased baseline mutation, more frequent and larger clonal expansions, impaired B-cell selection, and a shift toward the memory compartment (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered more frequent and larger clonal expansions with age.
source: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a number of important age-related changes, including reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences, increased baseline mutation, more frequent and larger clonal expansions, impaired B-cell selection, and a shift toward the memory compartment (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered impaired B-cell selection with age.
source: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a number of important age-related changes, including reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences, increased baseline mutation, more frequent and larger clonal expansions, impaired B-cell selection, and a shift toward the memory compartment (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a shift toward the memory compartment with age.
source: In humans, antibody-repertoire sequencing has uncovered a number of important age-related changes, including reduced numbers of clones and unique sequences, increased baseline mutation, more frequent and larger clonal expansions, impaired B-cell selection, and a shift toward the memory compartment (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: The responsiveness of the peripheral repertoire to vaccination is impaired during aging.
source: The responsiveness of the peripheral repertoire to vaccination is also impaired during aging (de Bourcy et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Within-individual repertoire diversity declines with age in humans.
source: While within-individual repertoire diversity declines with age, between-individual variability increases, with repertoires from older individuals differing more from one another than those from young individuals (de Bourcy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: Between-individual variability in repertoires increases with age in humans.
source: While within-individual repertoire diversity declines with age, between-individual variability increases, with repertoires from older individuals differing more from one another than those from young individuals (de Bourcy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous human studies.

claim: Previous work in humans has been limited by small sample sizes, lack of temporal resolution, or restriction to peripheral blood samples.
source: Previous work in humans, however, has been limited by small sample sizes, a lack of temporal resolution, or a restriction to peripheral blood samples, which are known to systematically underrepresent the majority of B-cells resident in other organs and tissues (Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009; Tabibian-Keissar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature.

claim: Peripheral blood samples systematically underrepresent the majority of B-cells resident in other organs and tissues.
source: Previous work in humans, however, has been limited by small sample sizes, a lack of temporal resolution, or a restriction to peripheral blood samples, which are known to systematically underrepresent the majority of B-cells resident in other organs and tissues (Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009; Tabibian-Keissar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Very little is known about how repertoire aging differs between distinct organs.
source: Very little is known about how repertoire aging differs between distinct organs
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on literature review.

claim: Almost nothing is known about how aging affects antibody repertoires at mucosal surfaces.
source: in particular, almost nothing is known about how aging affects antibody repertoires at mucosal surfaces, which represent a crucial interface between the body and its microbial environment (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Magadan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on literature review.

claim: Mucosal surfaces represent a crucial interface between the body and its microbial environment.
source: in particular, almost nothing is known about how aging affects antibody repertoires at mucosal surfaces, which represent a crucial interface between the body and its microbial environment (Belkaid and Hand, 2014; Magadan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Even less is known about how aging might affect the antibody repertoires of vertebrates other than mice and humans.
source: Even less is known about how aging might affect the antibody repertoires of vertebrates other than mice and humans.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on literature review.

claim: This study performs the first immune-repertoire sequencing experiments in turquoise killifish.
source: Here, we perform the first immune-repertoire sequencing experiments in this species
evidence: The authors explicitly state this is the first such study.

claim: Adult killifish express diverse and individualized heavy-chain repertoires.
source: demonstrating that adult killifish express diverse and individualized heavy-chain repertoires that undergo rapid loss of diversity with age.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing data and diversity analysis.

claim: Killifish heavy-chain repertoires undergo rapid loss of diversity with age.
source: demonstrating that adult killifish express diverse and individualized heavy-chain repertoires that undergo rapid loss of diversity with age.
evidence: This is shown by the alpha-diversity spectra analysis across age groups.

claim: The age-dependent loss of antibody-repertoire diversity primarily affects the composition of expanded clones.
source: The age-dependent loss of the antibody-repertoire diversity primarily affects the composition of expanded clones, with small naïve clones exhibiting much smaller age-related changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing diversity changes in large vs. small clones.

claim: Small naïve clones exhibit much smaller age-related changes than expanded clones.
source: The age-dependent loss of the antibody-repertoire diversity primarily affects the composition of expanded clones, with small naïve clones exhibiting much smaller age-related changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing diversity changes in large vs. small clones in Figure 2.

claim: The killifish intestinal antibody repertoire exhibits much more dramatic age-dependent diversity loss than the body as a whole.
source: By sequencing the repertoires of isolated intestinal samples, we further find that the killifish intestinal antibody repertoire exhibits much more dramatic age-dependent diversity loss than the body as a whole
evidence: This is shown by comparing intestinal and whole-body diversity spectra in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The dramatic intestinal diversity loss is possibly due to a much higher prevalence of expanded clones in the intestine.
source: possibly due to a much higher prevalence of expanded clones in the intestine
evidence: This is inferred from rarefaction analysis showing fewer small clones in intestinal samples.

claim: Loss of intestinal diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating reduced B-cell activity.
source: and that this loss of diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating reduced B-cell activity.
evidence: This is shown by gene set enrichment analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Independent repertoires from the same individual showed a high degree of similarity in their clonal composition.
source: Independent repertoires from the same individual showed a high degree of similarity in their clonal composition, with an average inter-replicate correlation in clone size of r = 0.89 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pilot replication experiment data.

claim: The average inter-replicate correlation in clone size was r = 0.89.
source: Independent repertoires from the same individual showed a high degree of similarity in their clonal composition, with an average inter-replicate correlation in clone size of r = 0.89 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pilot replication experiment.

claim: The protocol is capable of accurately and reproducibly reconstructing the expressed heavy-chain repertoires of individual killifish.
source: demonstrating that this protocol is capable of accurately and reproducibly reconstructing the expressed heavy-chain repertoires of individual killifish.
evidence: This is inferred from the high inter-replicate correlation and RDI clustering results.

claim: The clonal diversity of the whole-body killifish repertoire exhibited a significant decline with age at high diversity orders.
source: The clonal diversity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) of the whole-body killifish repertoire exhibited a significant decline with age (p < 0.05) at high diversity orders (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3)
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of diversity spectra across age groups.

claim: High-order clonal diversity decline indicates a significant and extremely rapid age-related decline in the diversity of the largest B-cell clones.
source: indicating a significant and extremely rapid age-related decline in the diversity of the largest B-cell clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the interpretation of high-order diversity measures.

claim: Lower-order clonal diversity exhibited no significant change with age.
source: In contrast, lower-order clonal diversity exhibited no significant change with age
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of diversity spectra at low orders.

claim: The overall composition of the whole-body repertoire remains relatively unchanged with age.
source: suggesting that the overall composition of the whole-body repertoire remains relatively unchanged.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in low-order clonal diversity.

claim: The B-cell clonal repertoire is overwhelmingly dominated by small, predominantly naïve clones.
source: Since the B-cell clonal repertoire is overwhelmingly dominated by small, predominantly naïve clones (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is shown by the cumulative clone-size distributions.

claim: Low-order clonal diversity measurements are primarily driven by changes in the diversity of small clones.
source: low-order clonal diversity measurements are primarily driven by changes in the diversity of small clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the interpretation of Hill diversity measures and clone-size distributions.

claim: The composition of small clones in the killifish antibody repertoire is much less sensitive to the effects of aging than that of large, expanded clones.
source: As such, these results indicate that the composition of small clones in the killifish antibody repertoire is much less sensitive to the effects of aging than that of large, expanded clones.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing diversity changes in small vs. large clones.

claim: The VJ diversity of the killifish repertoire exhibited no significant age-related change at any diversity order.
source: In contrast with the rapid age-related declines observed in high-order clonal diversity, the VJ diversity of the killifish repertoire exhibited no significant age-related change at any diversity order (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of VJ diversity spectra.

claim: Even the largest V/J combinations in each age group are overwhelmingly dominated by small clones.
source: Examining the clone-size distribution of each V/J combination (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B) revealed that even the largest V/J combinations in each age group are overwhelmingly dominated by small clones
evidence: This is shown by plotting V/J combinations against clone sizes.

claim: Both small and large clones in isolation showed a significant age effect on VJ diversity.
source: While both small and large clones in isolation showed a significant age effect on VJ diversity, the relative reduction in VJ alpha diversity with age was dramatically stronger for large clones
evidence: This is shown by analyzing VJ diversity separately for small and large clones.

claim: The relative reduction in VJ alpha diversity with age was dramatically stronger for large clones than small clones.
source: While both small and large clones in isolation showed a significant age effect on VJ diversity, the relative reduction in VJ alpha diversity with age was dramatically stronger for large clones, an effect observed across all diversity orders (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown by comparing VJ diversity ratios for large vs. small clones.

claim: The repertoire diversity of large (expanded) clones in the killifish whole-body repertoire is far more age-sensitive than that of small (predominantly naïve) clones.
source: As suggested by the clonal-diversity results, therefore, the repertoire diversity of large (expanded) clones in the killifish whole-body repertoire appears to be far more age-sensitive than that of small (predominantly naïve) clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined clonal and VJ diversity analyses.

claim: VJ beta-diversity spectra indicated a large age-related increase in beta diversity across a wide range of diversity orders.
source: In our dataset, VJ beta-diversity spectra (Appendix 1) indicated a large age-related increase in beta diversity across a wide range of diversity orders (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is shown by the beta-diversity spectra analysis.

claim: Older killifish exhibited significantly greater pairwise RDI distances.
source: Concordantly, older killifish also exhibited significantly greater pairwise RDI distances (Bolen et al., 2017), indicating progressive divergence in repertoire composition (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is shown by RDI distance analysis.

claim: Younger killifish exhibit antibody repertoires that are significantly more similar to one another.
source: As in humans, therefore, younger killifish exhibit antibody repertoires that are significantly more similar to one another, which then become increasingly distinct and individualized as the cohort increases in age.
evidence: This is shown by RDI distance and PCoA analysis.

claim: Killifish repertoires become increasingly distinct and individualized as the cohort increases in age.
source: As in humans, therefore, younger killifish exhibit antibody repertoires that are significantly more similar to one another, which then become increasingly distinct and individualized as the cohort increases in age.
evidence: This is shown by beta-diversity and RDI analysis.

claim: The human generative process has an estimated Shannon entropy of roughly 70 bits.
source: Excluding nonfunctional sequences, the human generative process has an estimated Shannon entropy of roughly 70 bits, corresponding to a first-order Hill diversity of roughly 1021 possible unique sequences (Elhanati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The human generative process corresponds to a first-order Hill diversity of roughly 10^21 possible unique sequences.
source: Excluding nonfunctional sequences, the human generative process has an estimated Shannon entropy of roughly 70 bits, corresponding to a first-order Hill diversity of roughly 1021 possible unique sequences (Elhanati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The total raw entropy for the killifish generative repertoire is roughly 33 bits.
source: Using this model, we estimated a total raw entropy for the killifish generative repertoire of roughly 33 bits (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: Roughly 8 bits of killifish generative entropy arise from variability in VDJ segment choice.
source: Of these 33 bits, roughly 8 arise from variability in VDJ segment choice, 12 from variability in the number and composition of junctional N-insertions, and 11 from P-insertions and deletions.
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: Roughly 12 bits of killifish generative entropy arise from variability in the number and composition of junctional N-insertions.
source: Of these 33 bits, roughly 8 arise from variability in VDJ segment choice, 12 from variability in the number and composition of junctional N-insertions, and 11 from P-insertions and deletions.
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: Roughly 11 bits of killifish generative entropy arise from P-insertions and deletions.
source: Of these 33 bits, roughly 8 arise from variability in VDJ segment choice, 12 from variability in the number and composition of junctional N-insertions, and 11 from P-insertions and deletions.
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: Accounting for convergent production and nonfunctional sequences reduced the initial raw entropy estimate by 10 bits.
source: Accounting for convergent production of identical sequences via different recombination events, and for events that give rise to nonfunctional nucleotide sequences (e.g. due to frame shift) reduced this initial raw estimate by 10 bits.
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: Before initial selection in the primary lymphoid organs, the killifish generative process has an estimated Shannon entropy of roughly 23 bits.
source: Before initial selection in the primary lymphoid organs, therefore, the killifish generative process has an estimated Shannon entropy of roughly 23 bits (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is calculated from the IGoR generative model.

claim: The killifish generative process corresponds to a first-order Hill diversity of roughly 10^7 possible unique sequences.
source: corresponding to a first-order Hill diversity of roughly 107 possible unique sequences.
evidence: This is calculated from the Shannon entropy estimate.

claim: The killifish generative process is capable of generating highly individualized IGH repertoires.
source: This nevertheless represents a highly complex and sophisticated system capable of generating highly individualized IGH repertoires.
evidence: This is inferred from the generative diversity analysis and inter-individual variability.

claim: The potential generative diversity of the killifish repertoire is vastly lower than in humans.
source: While impressive, the potential generative diversity of the killifish repertoire is nevertheless vastly lower than in humans, with a difference in productive generative entropy of almost 50 bits (Elhanati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing killifish and human generative entropies.

claim: The difference in productive generative entropy between killifish and humans is almost 50 bits.
source: While impressive, the potential generative diversity of the killifish repertoire is nevertheless vastly lower than in humans, with a difference in productive generative entropy of almost 50 bits (Elhanati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing killifish and human generative entropies.

claim: All components of the generative process exhibit lower entropies in killifish than in humans.
source: While all components of the generative process exhibit lower entropies in killifish than in humans, by far the greatest difference lies in the junctional N-insertions
evidence: This is inferred from comparing generative model parameters.

claim: The greatest difference in generative entropy between killifish and humans lies in the junctional N-insertions.
source: While all components of the generative process exhibit lower entropies in killifish than in humans, by far the greatest difference lies in the junctional N-insertions, which contribute almost 40 bits more to the generative entropy of the human repertoire than that of killifish.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing N-insertion contributions in both species.

claim: Junctional N-insertions contribute almost 40 bits more to the generative entropy of the human repertoire than that of killifish.
source: While all components of the generative process exhibit lower entropies in killifish than in humans, by far the greatest difference lies in the junctional N-insertions, which contribute almost 40 bits more to the generative entropy of the human repertoire than that of killifish.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing N-insertion contributions in both species.

claim: In humans, N-insertion distributions peak at around 5 nt per junction and often yield insertions of 10–20 nt.
source: The difference in the productive generative entropy between killifish and human arises from the distributions of N-insertions inferred from killifish and human data: in humans, these distributions peak at around 5 nt per junction and often yield insertions of 10–20 nt (Elhanati et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In killifish, the N-insertion distribution peaks at 0 nt per junction.
source: while in killifish the insertion distribution peaks at 0 nt per junction, and sequences with more than 5 nt of insertions at either junction are very rare (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the inferred N-insertion distributions.

claim: In killifish, sequences with more than 5 nt of N-insertions at either junction are very rare.
source: while in killifish the insertion distribution peaks at 0 nt per junction, and sequences with more than 5 nt of insertions at either junction are very rare (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by the inferred N-insertion distributions.

claim: N-insertions are the dominant source of sequence diversity in human repertoires.
source: Since N-insertions are the dominant source of sequence diversity in human repertoires, the large reduction in N-insertions in killifish relative to humans unsurprisingly results in a much lower overall generative diversity for the killifish adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human repertoires.

claim: The large reduction in N-insertions in killifish relative to humans results in a much lower overall generative diversity for the killifish adaptive immune system.
source: Since N-insertions are the dominant source of sequence diversity in human repertoires, the large reduction in N-insertions in killifish relative to humans unsurprisingly results in a much lower overall generative diversity for the killifish adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing N-insertion contributions to generative diversity.

claim: No age effect was found in total generative diversity in killifish.
source: As expected, no age effect was found in either total generative diversity (Figure 3D) or the contributions of different diversification processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of generative models across age groups.

claim: No age effect was found in the contributions of different diversification processes in killifish.
source: As expected, no age effect was found in either total generative diversity (Figure 3D) or the contributions of different diversification processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of generative model parameters across age groups.

claim: The entropy of the generative process does not decline with age in killifish.
source: It therefore appears that, while some aspects of the killifish antibody repertoire certainly decline with age, the entropy of the generative process is not among them.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of age effect on generative diversity.

claim: The populations of B-lymphocytes associated with mucosal epithelia play a crucial role in defending the body from pathogenic threats.
source: The populations of B-lymphocytes associated with mucosal epithelia play a crucial role in defending the body from pathogenic threats (Magadan et al., 2019), as well as in regulating the composition of resident microbial populations (Belkaid and Hand, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Mucosal B-lymphocytes play a role in regulating the composition of resident microbial populations.
source: The populations of B-lymphocytes associated with mucosal epithelia play a crucial role in defending the body from pathogenic threats (Magadan et al., 2019), as well as in regulating the composition of resident microbial populations (Belkaid and Hand, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Relatively little is known about the structure of mucosal B-cell antibody repertoires.
source: Despite the importance of these distinctive B-cell compartments, relatively little is known about the structure of their antibody repertoires (Magadan et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on literature review.

claim: Still less is known about how mucosal B-cell repertoires change with age.
source: and still less about how these repertoires change with age.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on literature review.

claim: The intestine is the site of the greatest microbiota diversity.
source: As the site of the greatest microbiota diversity, the intestine is of particular relevance as an important and distinctive immune environment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gut microbiome.

claim: The killifish gut microbiota declines in alpha diversity with age.
source: Previous work on the killifish gut microbiota (Smith et al., 2017) has shown that it declines in alpha diversity and increases in beta diversity with age
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The killifish gut microbiota increases in beta diversity with age.
source: Previous work on the killifish gut microbiota (Smith et al., 2017) has shown that it declines in alpha diversity and increases in beta diversity with age
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Patterns of microbiota diversity change with age mirror the changes seen in the whole-body composition of the killifish antibody repertoire.
source: patterns that mirror the changes seen in the whole-body composition of the killifish antibody repertoire (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing microbiota and repertoire diversity patterns.

claim: Transfer of intestinal content from young to middle-aged fish extends lifespan.
source: Transfer of intestinal content from young to middle-aged fish has also been shown to extend lifespan (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Neither the alpha nor beta diversity of the killifish intestinal repertoire were significantly affected by microbiota transfer.
source: Contrary to our expectations, neither the alpha nor beta diversity of the killifish intestinal repertoire were significantly affected by microbiota transfer, with no significant difference in clonal diversity, VJ diversity, or RDI distance measures (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of diversity measures across treatment groups.

claim: There was a strong and significant decline in both clonal and VJ alpha diversity with age in the intestine across all diversity orders.
source: In sharp contrast to the whole-body data, however, there was a strong and significant decline in both clonal and VJ alpha diversity with age across all diversity orders (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3), even without partitioning by clone size.
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing of intestinal diversity spectra.

claim: The age-related decline in intestinal alpha diversity was consistently far more dramatic than that observed in the whole-body samples at any diversity order.
source: This age-related decline in alpha diversity was consistently far more dramatic than that observed in the whole-body samples at any diversity order.
evidence: This is shown by comparing intestinal and whole-body diversity spectra.

claim: The B-cells of the killifish intestine exhibit a much stronger age-dependent decline in repertoire diversity than is seen in the killifish body overall.
source: The B-cells of the killifish intestine, therefore, exhibit a much stronger age-dependent decline in repertoire diversity than is seen in the killifish body overall.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing intestinal and whole-body diversity changes.

claim: The median pairwise RDI distance between individual gut repertoires increased substantially and significantly with age.
source: While results from beta-diversity spectra showed large increases in beta diversity with age at some diversity orders but not at others (Figure 4D), the median pairwise RDI distance between­ individual gut repertoires increased substantially and significantly with age (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is shown by RDI distance analysis of intestinal samples.

claim: Killifish intestinal repertoires become increasingly distinct and individualized as they age.
source: suggesting that, as in the whole body, killifish intestinal repertoires become increasingly distinct and individualized as they age.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in RDI distances with age.

claim: Constant strong antigen exposure experienced by intestinal B-cells could drive high levels of antigen-dependent clonal expansion.
source: One potential explanation for the stronger age-related drop in alpha diversity of intestinal samples is as a consequence of the constant strong antigen exposure experienced by intestinal B-cells, as a result of their interaction with the gut microbiota. This exposure could drive high levels of antigen-dependent clonal expansion, resulting in a greater loss in repertoire diversity (Caruso et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation cited from previous literature.

claim: The gut has a different clone-size distribution relative to the whole body.
source: Another explanation, not mutually exclusive with the first, is that the gut has different clone-size distribution relative to the whole body.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is then tested with data.

claim: The gut does not include the primary lymphoid organs.
source: Unlike the whole-body repertoire, the gut does not include the primary lymphoid organs, and so would be expected to be far less dominated by small, naïve clones.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The gut would be expected to be far less dominated by small, naïve clones than the whole body.
source: Unlike the whole-body repertoire, the gut does not include the primary lymphoid organs, and so would be expected to be far less dominated by small, naïve clones.
evidence: This is inferred from anatomical knowledge.

claim: Intestinal repertoires contained far fewer small clones than whole-body repertoires.
source: Rarefaction analysis of clonal counts in whole-body and intestinal repertoires showed that the latter indeed contained far fewer small clones, resulting in a much higher proportion of large clones (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by rarefaction analysis.

claim: Intestinal repertoires have a much higher proportion of large clones than whole-body repertoires.
source: Rarefaction analysis of clonal counts in whole-body and intestinal repertoires showed that the latter indeed contained far fewer small clones, resulting in a much higher proportion of large clones (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by rarefaction analysis.

claim: Gut samples exhibited significantly higher rates of age-dependent diversity loss under low-order clonal-diversity or total VJ-diversity measures.
source: Gut samples exhibited significantly higher rates of age-dependent diversity loss under low-order clonal-diversity or total VJ-diversity measures, that is, those metrics for which clones of all sizes were included in the diversity calculation.
evidence: This is shown by generalized linear model analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant difference in rate of diversity loss between gut and whole-body sample types for higher-order clonal-diversity measures.
source: Conversely, there was no significant difference in rate of diversity loss between sample types for higher-order clonal-diversity measures, nor for V/J-diversity measures restricted to only large clones
evidence: This is shown by generalized linear model analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant difference in rate of diversity loss between gut and whole-body sample types for V/J-diversity measures restricted to only large clones.
source: Conversely, there was no significant difference in rate of diversity loss between sample types for higher-order clonal-diversity measures, nor for V/J-diversity measures restricted to only large clones
evidence: This is shown by generalized linear model analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Large clones undergo similar rates of age-dependent diversity loss in both gut and whole-body samples.
source: indicating that large clones undergo similar rates of age-dependent diversity loss in both sample types.
evidence: This is inferred from the GLM analysis results.

claim: Large clones in both gut and whole-body samples exhibit similarly strong aging phenotypes.
source: These results closely match the predictions of the clonal-composition model: large clones in both gut and whole-body samples exhibit similarly strong aging phenotypes, but the higher proportions of large clones in gut samples result in these strong phenotypes manifesting more strongly in the behavior of the repertoire as a whole.
evidence: This is inferred from the GLM and rarefaction analysis results.

claim: The higher proportions of large clones in gut samples result in strong aging phenotypes manifesting more strongly in the behavior of the repertoire as a whole.
source: These results closely match the predictions of the clonal-composition model: large clones in both gut and whole-body samples exhibit similarly strong aging phenotypes, but the higher proportions of large clones in gut samples result in these strong phenotypes manifesting more strongly in the behavior of the repertoire as a whole.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of clone composition and diversity changes.

claim: Age-dependent diversity loss in killifish intestinal repertoires is primarily a phenomenon of mature, expanded clones.
source: It therefore appears that, as in whole-body samples, age-dependent diversity loss in killifish intestinal repertoires is primarily a phenomenon of mature, expanded clones.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of clone-size effects on diversity changes.

claim: Early work in killifish identified thymic degeneration as an age-associated phenotype.
source: Early work in killifish identified a number of age-associated phenotypes suggestive of immune decline, including thymic degeneration and increased incidence of lymphoma (Cooper et al., 1983).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Early work in killifish identified increased incidence of lymphoma as an age-associated phenotype.
source: Early work in killifish identified a number of age-associated phenotypes suggestive of immune decline, including thymic degeneration and increased incidence of lymphoma (Cooper et al., 1983).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Comparison of young vs. old killifish intestines found a marked age-related increase in the pathogenicity of the killifish gut microbiome.
source: More recently, comparison of young vs. old killifish intestines found a marked age-related increase in the pathogenicity of the killifish gut microbiome, alongside an increase in expression of inflammatory markers, suggesting a decline in the intestinal immune system's ability to maintain a healthy microbial community (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Comparison of young vs. old killifish intestines found an increase in expression of inflammatory markers.
source: More recently, comparison of young vs. old killifish intestines found a marked age-related increase in the pathogenicity of the killifish gut microbiome, alongside an increase in expression of inflammatory markers, suggesting a decline in the intestinal immune system's ability to maintain a healthy microbial community (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The turquoise killifish undergoes rapid functional immune decline with age.
source: These results suggest that the turquoise killifish undergoes rapid functional immune decline with age.
evidence: This is inferred from cited previous findings.

claim: Markers of functional immune decline are coincident with a reduction in repertoire diversity in killifish.
source: Since repertoire diversity also declines with age, this indicates that markers of functional immune decline are coincident with a reduction in repertoire diversity.
evidence: This is inferred from combining previous findings with current results.

claim: B-cell receptor signaling pathway was the most strongly enriched term for all six diversity orders analyzed in the GSEA.
source: Most strikingly, 'B-cell receptor signaling pathway' was the most strongly enriched term for all six diversity orders analyzed, often by a substantial margin.
evidence: This is shown by the GSEA results in Figure 6.

claim: B-cell proliferation showed significant positive enrichment for five diversity orders in the GSEA.
source: 'B-cell proliferation' was also consistently highly enriched, showing significant positive enrichment for five diversity orders (all except 1.0) and falling in the top 10 most positively enriched terms for four (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown by the GSEA results in Figure 6.

claim: A decline in repertoire diversity is associated with a decline in B-cell immune activity in killifish intestine.
source: A decline in repertoire diversity is thus associated with a decline in B-cell immune activity in killifish intestine, supporting a functional role for diversity changes in killifish immunosenescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA results showing enrichment of immune terms.

claim: The turquoise killifish is the shortest-lived vertebrate that can be bred in captivity.
source: The turquoise killifish is the shortest-lived vertebrate that can be bred in captivity (Cellerino et al., 2016; Harel and Brunet, 2015)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The median lifespan of the short-lived GRZ strain is about 4 months.
source: with a median lifespan in the short-lived GRZ strain of about 4 months.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GRZ strain.

claim: The life of a turquoise killifish provides ample time to develop a complex, diverse, and individualized IgM heavy-chain repertoire.
source: Despite this, our findings show that the life of a turquoise killifish provides ample time both to develop a complex, diverse, and individualized IgM heavy-chain repertoire (Figure 3A, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequencing and diversity analysis results.

claim: The life of a turquoise killifish provides ample time for the repertoire to decline significantly in diversity with age.
source: and for that repertoire to decline significantly in diversity with age.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the age-series diversity analysis.

claim: Age-associated diversity changes in killifish appear to be driven primarily by expanded, antigen-experienced clones.
source: These age-associated diversity changes appear to be driven primarily by expanded, antigen-experienced clones, with little observed change in either the diversity of small naïve clones or the entropy of the heavy-chain sequence generation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the clone-size-stratified diversity analysis.

claim: There is little observed change in the diversity of small naïve clones with age in killifish.
source: These age-associated diversity changes appear to be driven primarily by expanded, antigen-experienced clones, with little observed change in either the diversity of small naïve clones or the entropy of the heavy-chain sequence generation process.
evidence: This is shown by the small-clone diversity analysis.

claim: There is little observed change in the entropy of the heavy-chain sequence generation process with age in killifish.
source: These age-associated diversity changes appear to be driven primarily by expanded, antigen-experienced clones, with little observed change in either the diversity of small naïve clones or the entropy of the heavy-chain sequence generation process.
evidence: This is shown by the generative model analysis across ages.

claim: It is possible that a decline in efficiency of B-cell output from primary lymphoid organs is offset by the continuous growth in body size observed throughout the killifish lifespan.
source: This lack of change in small-clone diversity, however, does not necessarily imply that B-cell development is unchanged in aging killifish: it is possible, for example, that a decline in efficiency of B-cell output from primary lymphoid organs is offset by the continuous growth in body size observed throughout the killifish lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: Caruso et al., 2009, hypothesized that the mucosal adaptive immune system might exhibit particularly strong loss of diversity with age.
source: As early as 2009, Caruso et al., 2009, hypothesized that the mucosal adaptive immune system might exhibit particularly strong loss of diversity with age.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: This is the first published test of the hypothesis that mucosal adaptive immune systems exhibit particularly strong loss of diversity with age.
source: In what is, to our knowledge, the first published test of this hypothesis, we sequenced the heavy-chain repertoires of isolated killifish gut samples, finding that they do indeed exhibit particularly strong diversity changes with age.
evidence: The authors state this is the first test of this hypothesis.

claim: Killifish gut samples exhibit particularly strong diversity changes with age.
source: In what is, to our knowledge, the first published test of this hypothesis, we sequenced the heavy-chain repertoires of isolated killifish gut samples, finding that they do indeed exhibit particularly strong diversity changes with age.
evidence: This is shown by the intestinal repertoire analysis.

claim: The difference between gut and whole-body repertoires appears to result from a difference in clonal composition, rather than in the behavior of any particular clonal subset.
source: However, this difference between the gut and whole-body repertoires appears to result from a difference in clonal composition, rather than in the behavior of any particular clonal subset
evidence: This is inferred from the rarefaction and GLM analysis.

claim: The difference in aging between gut and whole-body may have less to do with the specifics of the mucosal environment than the location of the primary lymphoid organs.
source: suggesting this difference may have less to do with the specifics of the mucosal environment than the location of the primary lymphoid organs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Age-dependent loss of mucosal repertoire diversity could have important consequences for the gut's capacity to respond to novel antigens.
source: Whatever its source, this age-dependent loss of mucosal repertoire diversity could have important consequences for the gut's capacity to respond to novel antigens.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential functional consequences.

claim: Greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater B-cell receptor signaling activity.
source: Gene expression data from our intestinal cohort indicates that greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater B-cell receptor signaling activity, lymphocyte activation, and defense responses
evidence: This is shown by the GSEA analysis.

claim: Greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater lymphocyte activation.
source: Gene expression data from our intestinal cohort indicates that greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater B-cell receptor signaling activity, lymphocyte activation, and defense responses
evidence: This is shown by the GSEA analysis.

claim: Greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater defense responses.
source: Gene expression data from our intestinal cohort indicates that greater intestinal repertoire diversity is associated with gene expression changes indicating greater B-cell receptor signaling activity, lymphocyte activation, and defense responses
evidence: This is shown by the GSEA analysis.

claim: The decline in diversity seen with age is associated with a decline in immune function.
source: suggesting that the decline in diversity seen with age is associated with a decline in immune function.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA results.

claim: The associations between diversity and immune function support the biological relevance of repertoire diversity as a metric of immune function.
source: While not necessarily causal, these associations support the biological relevance of repertoire diversity as a metric of immune function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GSEA results.

claim: No other system in the vertebrate body exhibits such complex learning and memory behavior as the adaptive immune system, apart from the nervous system.
source: Apart from the nervous system itself, no other system in the vertebrate body exhibits such complex learning and memory behavior as the adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge.

claim: The age-related decline in the functionality of the adaptive immune system is a major cause of mortality and morbidity in the elderly.
source: The age-related decline in the functionality of this system is a major cause of mortality and morbidity in the elderly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about immunosenescence.

claim: The results firmly establish the value of the turquoise killifish as a model for investigating adaptive immunosenescence.
source: Our results firmly establish the value of the turquoise killifish as a model for investigating this important and complex process
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The results demonstrate the importance of studying immune aging in compartments other than peripheral blood.
source: and demonstrate the importance of studying immune aging in compartments other than peripheral blood.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences observed between whole-body and intestinal repertoires.

claim: The immunoglobulin sequencing protocol uses template switching to add unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) to each RNA transcript.
source: we implemented an RNA-based repertoire-sequencing protocol based on the published protocol of Turchaninova et al., 2016, using template switching (Zajac et al., 2013) to add unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) to each RNA transcript of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (Figure 1; Bradshaw and Valenzano, 2020) to correct for errors and biases in abundance arising during PCR and Illumina sequencing (Vollmers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: UMIs are used to correct for errors and biases in abundance arising during PCR and Illumina sequencing.
source: using template switching (Zajac et al., 2013) to add unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) to each RNA transcript of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (Figure 1; Bradshaw and Valenzano, 2020) to correct for errors and biases in abundance arising during PCR and Illumina sequencing (Vollmers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established methodology cited from previous literature.

claim: Inter-repertoire divergences computed with the RDI metric consistently identified replicates from the same individual as much more similar than repertoires from different individuals.
source: Inter-repertoire divergences computed with the published repertoire dissimilarity index (RDI) metric (Bolen et al., 2017) consistently identified replicates from the same individual as much more similar than repertoires from different individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is shown by the RDI clustering analysis in the pilot experiment.

claim: Male turquoise killifish from a single hatching cohort were raised under standard husbandry conditions.
source: Male turquoise killifish (N. furzeri, GRZ-AD strain) from a single hatching cohort were raised under standard husbandry conditions (Dodzian et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Fish were housed from 4 weeks' post-hatching in individual 2.8 l tanks connected to a water-recirculation system.
source: and housed from 4 weeks' post-hatching in individual 2.8 l tanks connected to a water-recirculation system.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Fish received 12 hr of light per day on a regular light/dark cycle.
source: Fish received 12 hr of light per day on a regular light/dark cycle
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
